extracted.intended_audience: USCIS officers, immigration practitioners (attorneys/advocates), and noncitizen applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory standards and procedural guidance for determining whether a noncitizen is "likely at any time to become a public charge" under INA section 212(a)(4), including definitions, factors to consider, evidentiary sources, exclusions, procedural requirements (denials, forms), and bond rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "public charge" (primary criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A noncitizen is considered likely at any time to become a public charge if the noncitizen is likely at any time to become primarily dependent on the government for subsistence, as demonstrated by either (1) the receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance, or (2) long-term institutionalization at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule hews to the 1999 Interim Field Guidance approach and rejects the broader 2019 Final Rule definition. The term is tied to being "primarily dependent" (significant reliance), not mere receipt of supplemental benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of "primarily dependent"
rubrics_metrics.description: "Primary dependence" connotes significant reliance on the government for support, and means something more than dependence that is merely transient or supplementary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the threshold concept for public charge determinations to distinguish individuals who primarily rely on government subsistence from those who secondarily or transiently rely on some government support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public cash assistance for income maintenance (benefits considered)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public cash assistance for income maintenance includes Supplemental Security Income (SSI), cash assistance for income maintenance under Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), and State, Tribal, territorial, or local cash benefit programs for income maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will consider receipt of these cash benefits as evidence of primary dependence. DHS intentionally limits the list of considered benefits to these cash programs (and long-term institutionalization) to reduce chilling effects and preserve administrability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term institutionalization at government expense (benefit considered)
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term institutionalization at government expense is considered a ground-demonstrating primary dependence. The regulatory text replaces the term 'alien' with 'beneficiary' to capture the forward-looking inquiry (including institutionalization that may occur after the applicant is no longer an 'alien').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term institutionalization is the non-cash benefit DHS treats as probative of primary dependence; the rule clarifies definitions and evidentiary scope for institutional care considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minimum factors to consider (general list)
rubrics_metrics.description: In making a public charge determination, DHS must consider at a minimum the alien's (1) age; (2) health; (3) family status; (4) assets, resources, and financial status; and (5) education and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the core statutory factors from the INA (8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(4)) that DHS must assess in the totality of the circumstances analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age (factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the noncitizen's age as part of the totality of the circumstances under the statutory minimum factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Age is a statutory factor; the preamble and regulatory text require officers to evaluate how age affects likelihood of becoming primarily dependent (e.g., elderly dependents, minors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Health (factor and evidence standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the noncitizen's health as evidenced by a report of an immigration medical examination performed by a civil surgeon or panel physician where such examination is required in making public charge inadmissibility determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will generally defer to the report of the examination unless there is evidence the report is incomplete. The rule also states that the fact an applicant has a disability (as defined by Section 504) would not alone be a sufficient basis to determine likely to become a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family status (factor; household definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider family status as evidenced by the noncitizen's household size; 'household' includes the noncitizen, spouse, parents, unmarried siblings under 21 and children if physically residing with the noncitizen, any individuals listed as dependents on the noncitizen's federal income tax return, and any individuals who list the noncitizen as a dependent on their federal income tax return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Household income includes income provided to the household from non-household members (e.g., alimony, child support). This definition is used when evaluating family status and assets/resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assets, resources, and financial status (factor; evidentiary scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the noncitizen's assets, resources, and financial status as evidenced by the noncitizen's household's income, assets, and liabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory text excludes income from public benefits listed in 8 CFR 212.21(b) and income or assets from illegal activities (e.g., proceeds from illegal gambling or drug sales). Officers should evaluate household-level finances, not just individual finances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and skills (factor; evidentiary scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the noncitizen's education and skills as evidenced by degrees, certifications, licenses, skills obtained through work experience or educational programs, and educational certificates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education and skills are evaluated for their bearing on employment prospects and ability to avoid dependence on public subsistence programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support under section 213A (consideration when applicable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The agencies may consider an Affidavit of Support under section 213A of the INA submitted on the noncitizen's behalf where such is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an affidavit of support is required, officers should consider it as part of the financial/resources evidence in the totality of circumstances analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of current and/or past receipt of designated public benefits (limited list)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider current and/or past receipt of the public benefits specifically referenced in the rule (public cash assistance for income maintenance and long-term institutionalization at government expense) in its totality of the circumstances analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS clarified regulatory text to state it will not consider receipt of, or certification or approval for future receipt of, public benefits not referenced in 8 CFR 212.21(b) or (c) (for example SNAP, CHIP, Medicaid (except for long-term institutionalization), housing benefits, immunizations/testing benefits, or other supplemental/special-purpose benefits). This choice is intended to focus on benefits most indicative of primary dependence and to limit chilling effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bright-line rule: do not consider benefits received by an applicant's dependents
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS states a bright-line rule against considering the receipt of public benefits by an applicant's dependents (such as a U.S. citizen child in a mixed-status household) when making a public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prohibition is intended to avoid penalizing applicants for dependents' benefit receipt and to mitigate collateral chilling effects on U.S. citizen children or other dependents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions and limited consideration (categories and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider public benefits received by a noncitizen during periods in which the noncitizen was present in the United States in an immigration category that is exempt from the public charge ground of inadmissibility, or for which the noncitizen received a waiver of public charge inadmissibility. DHS will also not consider public benefits received by a noncitizen who was made eligible by Congress for resettlement assistance, entitlement programs, or other refugee benefits, even if not admitted as a refugee under section 207.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule tailors consideration to avoid penalizing individuals who received benefits while in exempt statuses or as part of congressionally authorized resettlement/refugee programs. It also clarifies that certain categories (e.g., T nonimmigrants seeking adjustment) are not subject to the public charge ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances framework (assessment approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will evaluate likelihood to become a public charge under a totality of the circumstances framework, weighing statutory minimum factors, designated public benefits receipt, the Affidavit of Support where required, and other relevant information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble addresses recommendations about presumptions and weighting; DHS declined to adopt 'heavily weighted' factor designations like in the 2019 rule and emphasizes fair and consistent adjudications under the totality approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial decisions must articulate consideration of factors and reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposed (and the final text requires) that all written denial decisions issued by USCIS must reflect consideration of each of the statutory minimum factors, the Affidavit of Support where required, and the noncitizen's current and/or past receipt of public benefits, and must specifically articulate the reasons for the officer's determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides procedural transparency and ensures the officer addressed each statutory element when denying an application for visa/admission/adjustment based on public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form I-485 revisions (information collection requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS revised Form I-485 to collect additional information relevant to the public charge inadmissibility determination (questions regarding family status; assets, resources, and financial status; education and skills; and past receipt of designated public benefits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The additional questions apply only to applicants subject to the public charge ground and are intended to provide officers with standardized evidence for the statutory factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bonds: acceptance, form, and amount (bond criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS added streamlined provisions to clarify acceptance, form, and amount of USCIS public charge bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulatory amendments set forth criteria on how bonds are to be accepted, the required form, and calculation/expectations about amounts; these rules govern when bonds may be used instead of other admissibility outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bonds: cancellation and breach procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS amended procedures relating to cancellation and breach of public charge bonds, including clarifying grounds and procedures for cancellation and what constitutes breach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural rules define when bonds may be cancelled, how breaches are handled, and interactions with 8 CFR 103.6(c)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence/information deference rules (e.g., medical reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will generally defer to authoritative evidence such as immigration medical exam reports (civil surgeon/panel physician reports) unless there is evidence the report is incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers should rely on and defer to specified authoritative sources of evidence for particular statutory factors unless problems are shown with those sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of certain benefits from consideration (explicit non-consideration list)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS expressly states it will not consider SNAP, CHIP, Medicaid (except for long-term institutionalization), housing benefits, benefits related to immunizations/testing for communicable diseases, or other supplemental or special-purpose benefits in public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list is repeated and emphasized to limit chilling effects and to inform applicants and officers which benefits are not probative of primary dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disability consideration (non-dispositive guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS specifically states that the fact an applicant has a disability, as defined by Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, would not alone be a sufficient basis to determine whether the noncitizen is likely at any time to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disability must be evaluated in context with other factors; a disability alone cannot be the sole basis for finding likely to become a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing/applicability (effective date and application-postmark rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule is effective December 23, 2022, and will apply to applications postmarked on or after the effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural rule defines which filings are subject to the new public charge regulatory standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on considering certification/approval for future receipt of non-designated benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS clarified it will not consider the receipt of, or certification or approval for future receipt of, public benefits not referenced in the designated-benefits provisions (e.g., SNAP, Medicaid generally, housing vouchers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents speculative use of approvals/certifications for non-probative benefits as evidence of likely primary dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: No 'heavily weighted' factor designations
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike the 2019 Final Rule, DHS declined to designate certain factors or factual circumstances as 'heavily weighted' in the public charge determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS adopts a more balanced totality-of-the-circumstances approach and avoids rigid weightings that could create undue burdens or chilling effects.
